findings.obs_text: In Jer 3:19 the Lord's thought is of giving Israel a heritage most beautiful and being called Father: the heritage is the gift the thought intended.
findings.grounds: a heritage most beautiful of all nations

findings.obs_text: In 2Sa 10:3 and 1Ch 19:3 the princes ask Hanun whether he thinks David is honoring his father: the thought about honor is turned to suspicion. In Rom 1:21 not honoring God goes with futile thinking. In 1Cor 12:23 the parts thought less honorable are given more honor, and in 1Ti 3:7 being well thought of guards against disgrace.

older.finding: The original (§4.6a). The English sets "honor" (1:21) against "dishonoring" and "dishonorable" (1:24, 26). The Greek does not: "honor" in 1:21 is doxazō "glorify". "Dishonoring" (1:24) is atimazō and "dishonorable passions" (1:26) is pathē atimias, literally "passions of dishonor". Atimia is the negative of timē "honour" (M71). findings.obs_text: In Isa 59:7 the feet that are swift to shed innocent blood belong to those whose thoughts are thoughts of iniquity: the act and the thoughts are named together.

Intention and thought stand side by side in Gen 6:5, 1Ch 28:9 and 1Ch 29:18, where the same pair of words names the formed purpose and the thoughts of the heart; in Psa 64:5 the evil purpose goes with the quoted thought, and in Isa 10:7 the Assyrian does not so intend nor his heart so think. In Mic 4:12 the Lord's thoughts and his plan are unknown to the nations, in Heb 4:12 the word discerns thoughts and intentions, and in Joh 11:13 the disciples mistake what Jesus meant.
findings.grounds: every intention of the thoughts of his heart
